prompt:
You are advising BidThread, a B2B workflow SaaS that turns a commercial janitorial company's walkthrough notes and photos into an editable scope of work and proposal. Write a one-page operating memo for the founders. Decide which function should lead the next four weeks, diagnose the bottleneck from the evidence, recommend one bounded move, and leave an August 14, 2026 decision table the team can execute while the founders are offline. Do not ask for more data; label any assumptions.

BidThread has 16 months of runway. No safety, participant-policy, pricing, or packaging dispute is currently binding. The selected segment is US commercial janitorial companies with 10-50 employees, at least four property bids per month, and no dedicated estimator. The June 1-15 cohort came entirely from personalized cold email and has matured through week three. Forty-eight companies paid a non-refundable $600 six-week pilot fee without discounts; 42 then uploaded notes from a real, current property walkthrough.

The team set minimum acceptable step rates before the cohort started. Account-level results were: 400 cold-email recipients -> 160 watched the eight-minute demo (40%; floor 30%); 160 demo viewers -> 48 paid starts (30%; floor 20%); 48 paid starts -> 42 real walkthrough uploads (87.5%; floor 70%); 42 uploads -> 39 generated proposals (92.9%; floor 80%). The dashboard then reports 17 of those 39 as submitted to a live prospect (43.6%; floor 60%). A support audit shows that, for 11 of the 17, a founder spent 28 total hours rewriting the scope and formatting the PDF before handing it back; that labor was absent from product events. Only 6 of 39 accounts submitted without staff editing. Of those 6, 5 used BidThread for another proposal in week three (83.3%; floor 50%), and 2 of those 5 referred another qualified company (40%; floor 20%).

The next 20 paid accounts from the same segment and source will enroll July 20-31. All 20 will have seven full days to act before the review. The founders can spend at most ten total hours observing customer work; they may explain the product, but any staff editing or sending can be logged. Engineering can make one one-week workflow change after a concrete friction is observed. There is no budget for new automation or a second acquisition channel this month. Before enrollment, the board defined 13-20 independently activated accounts as a pass, 7-12 as repairable, and 0-6 as a stop signal. An account stays in the denominator even if staff rescues it.
criteria: The memo makes Growth/distribution the primary owner because non-discounted payment plus real current-work use has crossed the learning-to-growth handoff; it does not misroute the present decision to customer learning, product shipping, pricing, or survival.

The memo identifies generated proposal -> independently submitted live proposal as the first broken full-loop transition and measures the trustworthy rate as 6/39 = 15.4%, rather than treating the founder-assisted 17/39 as genuine activation.

The memo proposes a bounded manual-first intervention for the next 20 same-segment accounts and prevents hidden founder rescue from counting as success, for example by logging all help and counting only a later proposal submitted without staff editing or sending while rescued accounts remain in the denominator.
The memo schedules the review for August 14, 2026 and gives exhaustive numeric branches: pass at 13-20 independent activations, repair at 7-12, and stop at 0-6.

The memo assigns an explicit accountable next owner to every material branch: Growth for pass/replication, Shipping/Product for the repair before Growth reruns the cohort, and Customer Learning for the stop branch while acquisition expansion remains paused.
